saving the Rhino

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Its the biggest dehorning ever undertaken and we got to ride in on their final day

Summary:
For the past 5 years Nico J from Rhino 911 has been fighting with the government to implement a mass dehorning of the full rhino population in the Pilanesberg, which is a K1 population and one of the most important in the SADC region. He was stone walled for years, even after he offered to pay for the operation himself. Until this year. He was given the go ahead and immediately had to get sponsors on board to cover the 2 million rand operation.

It is the biggest operation of its kind ever undertaken in the world. Two helicopters with 15 people per team took 9 days to remove the horns of the entire rhino population. They have one day left, which we can fly in on with them.

Lockdown was the perfect time to do the operation, as the park was void of all tourists. But during the operation they battled to find a cow and her calf, only to eventually discover her fresh carcass on the parks border. The calf was never found. They were too late. This wasn’t new to Nico who has run smaller operations in parks across Africa. He says that every time they start an operation they lose at least one rhino, as the syndicates are tipped off.

Over the 9 days they removed over ¾ of a billion Rands worth of Rhino horn, which has now been placed in state vaults around the country.
- This may be angle too? It’s a debate we have all heard though, whether or not to legalise and control the trade of Rhino horn.

Nico documented the entire operation and has sent me the videos. He has some amazing footage.
The story would be about the magnitude of the operation and the humans that worked 15 hour days to get it done in order to save the Rhino the only way they know how.
- Can add an element of the debate around whether or not Dehorning the right solution though

Script:





Nico Jacobs and his team from the NGO Rhino 911 have dedicated their lives to fighting poaching. I got to join them on the biggest Rhino dehorning operation in the world. The mission was to dehorn the entire Rhino population of the Pilanesberg national park in 9 days. working in conjunction with the north west parks board it would take two helicopters, two vets and over 50 ground staff working against the clock to try and save these Rhino

derek:
So you envisage this project to dehorn the entire rhino population the Pilansberg but first you need money and then you need buy in from the Parks Board. How easily did it happen.
Derek it wasn't that easy we've been throwing the idea around and none of us actually ever wanted to see rhinos without horns. It's not it's not our preferred method.
we're not saying it's the ultimate solution but it's one method that's that's working for us at this stage.
NICO:
I truly believe we need to do everything in our power to give the animal the benefit of trying every single thing that we can do. And this has been proven to work.
But our biggest challenge was was finances. And as you know which that's however difficult to to raise funds.
we just put the word out there that we want to do this project it's highly secretive so a small group of people that we trusted with the information you know came to the party and we raised the funds.


This isn’t a cheap operation. It will come to About two million Rands. But that's just the price a single rhino horn gets on the black market.

The rhino population of the Pilanesberg is the third largest wild rhino population in the world and even though ecologist Steven Dell together with his anti-poaching task team have been fighting poachers day and night they have lost 150 rhino’s in 10 years

Steve:
It doesn't matter what you do they're going to get in
it's like all crime
I've been on 150 crime scenes. Some are babies some are you know where the baby is still alive or it's badly injured or we've got orphans We're tired of witnessing that.
there are hard days when you get this particular scenes when you get there and you say I've had enough. I mean I could walk away I will. And then you don't. you say okay tomorrow I'm going to do better and I'm going to get my guys more motivated and we're gonna change it.

From March to April this year alone the park they lost 4 Rhinos leaving behind orphaned calves, which Nico Jacobs and his team had to fly in and rescue

Upsound: Nico in the field with a calf talking about hoe she would be dead if they hadn’t found her

NICO
when the poaching increased I was called out more and more to assist with poaching incidents.
I've been at
hundreds and hundreds of poaching scenes
You get two terrible scenes where you know animals are spined over their spines, babies killed And some of those rhino poaching and hacking off the Horn actually happens while that animal is still alive

This was not the first dehorning operation for Rhino 911, they have done smaller projects in the north west province. Where they learnt that if poachers get wind of a dehorning they move in and take what they can.

NICO:
I think we left four rhinos in Botsulano when we went back six months later to do those four in that same week that we were on our way to do them. We lost three of them literally in a 24 hour period.

Time is of the essence in a massive undertaking like this, not only due to the danger of poaching, but also because of the interspeci threat

NICO:
You know for fighting and for you know females that do come on heat that the Bulls within fights a bull with a horn and a bull without a horn can be a problem. But basically we needed to get it done in the shortest time of period and I must say Covid actually helped us with that because there's no tourism tourists in the park. And you know that gave us the leverage to actually go forth and tackle this thing on a very entrusted secret mission.


The team worked 14 hour days to make sure that no Rhino was left at risk. I was only there for one of those days and found it exhausting, I don’t know how they maintained the pace.

NICO
We we are oiled we know how it works so we literally dart the animal trim the horn with under 10 minutes. So it's a fairly simple idea.
GV
it's a passion so you don't really feel the tiredness because it's something you want to do and you can see the benefits of this. So you just keep on carrying on

Gerhardus Scheepers was one of the vets on the operation, him and Nico have been working together for over 10 years.

GV
Once you've darted the rhino the team has got to move in quickly.
normally takes anything from about five to seven minutes from the minute the dart hit the animal till it's so asleep that you can actually work with the animal
GV
We saw you loading up what do you use and the darts basically we use a drug called M99 the active ingredient is etophine which is a synthetic morphine derivative
GV
That's about between seven to ten thousand times more potent than the morphine they're using human medication.

GV:
But now that horn starts growing from today.
Yes. That's growing from today. And normally we have to redo these operations in about 18 months
Verite: Derek and vet Is there a different procedure Btw the black and white rhino
White rhino is passive and black Rhino is aggressive

When the white Rhino we were working on woke up she immediately starting looking for her calf, Which was nowhere to be seen. But the team wanted to give her time to find her calf before they intervened


Verite: Gerhardus the vet talking about how they have to shave the horn off: Can’t cut into the blood supply

STEVE:
What happens to the horn or horns that we took off today.
I don't want to know.
they go straight to a secure location which I actually don't know where that is.

During this project almost 1 billions rands worth of Rhino horn was removed, catalogued, microchipped and placed in secure state vaults.

Again we're not saying it's the only solution and we're not saying it's the ultimate solution. And I can assure you they will still come and kill animals with that little bit of. But at least we giving the babies time to grow up

ON day two of this project the team was devastated to find the carcass of poached Rhino. Which cemented their commitment to dehorning as the most effective solution in the fight against Rhino poaching

Derek: when the vet is cutting off the horn. How does that make you feel.
Steve:
I'm personally saddened about the whole operation and where we've come. it literally got to a point when we would pass a rhino in a day and say I hope you're alive tomorrow.
And so if I can walk away now and saying you will be alive tomorrow then I'm happy.
Steve:
One rhino death is one too many.
We have to keep these animals alive for the next generations. We're old. We're on our way out. You know. But you know we're doing.
I'm not doing this to save the Rhino for me I'm doing it to save it for our grandchildren.

After the day was over Steve and Nico took to the sky to make sure the Rhino we dehorned and her calf had found each other. They located them back together in their usual spot. The job was done. After 9 gruelling days the entire population of black and white Rhino in the Pilanesberg had been dehorned.

Steve:
Steve would you say that the rhino that have been the dehorned are safe. safe is a is a is a big word.
Like we said it's a reward and risk scenario from criminals. They are certainly safer. But our our anti poaching efforts have to be maintained if not improved. Um so there's no slacking from our perspective.
